title: ServiceNow shifts contract pricing as artificial intelligence threatens enterprise software seats
subtitle: Analysts raised price targets across enterprise software, but shifting contracts away from human headcount remains unfinished.
summary: A wave of Wall Street upgrades met a muted tape as ServiceNow navigates the transition away from per-user software pricing. The company must prove its automation tools can expand contract values before slowing growth and high multiples catch up with the shares.

bodyHtml:
Wall Street spent Oct. 12 insisting that enterprise software has nothing to fear from artificial intelligence. RBC Capital pushed its own target sharply higher that morning, while Bank of America double-upgraded Salesforce on the thesis that AI bots strengthen legacy software. ServiceNow caught that tailwind, spiked at the open, and surrendered the entire move by the closing bell. That muted tape exposed an awkward disconnect: since the June close, the stock has climbed roughly 42% while next-twelve-month earnings estimates rose just 4%. Investors did not buy accelerating profits over the summer; they simply paid a steeper multiple for the same run rate.

To understand why buyers hesitated, look at what ServiceNow actually sells. Strip away the corporate jargon, and it is the digital plumbing under the enterprise help desk. When you start a job and request a laptop, flag an outage, or file an expense report, that ticket routes through ServiceNow. It organizes approvals across human resources, customer service, and finance for global corporations and federal agencies. Everyone assumes clients are buying ticketing software, but they are really buying the map. ServiceNow holds the governed record of who can touch which corporate asset, and under whose authority.

That map is why the company sits in the crosshairs of the agentic AI wave. For most of 2026, software investors worried that intelligent bots would obliterate the per-seat pricing model. If autonomous agents handle IT troubleshooting, a chief information officer will cancel those logins the way you cancel an unused gym membership. But bots cannot navigate an enterprise without guardrails. Any autonomous agent running on Microsoft Agent 365 still requires permissions to access core systems. ServiceNow launched its AI Control Tower to govern those agents rather than fight them, backed by its $2.85 billion purchase of Moveworks and its consumption-priced Flow service desk.

The real transition is happening inside customer contracts. At its May investor day, management disclosed that about half of net new annual contract value has already abandoned seat-based pricing. Fresh AI-native software bundles command a 20% to 30% price lift, while AI reasoning costs under 10% of what ServiceNow spends to deliver it. The company targets more than $30 billion in subscription revenue by 2030, projecting roughly 30% will stem from AI products. At a September investor conference, chief executive Bill McDermott claimed a single seat converts into roughly 4.5 times its original revenue over a contract life. That is a conference talking point rather than a reported metric, but it shows the goal: replace vulnerable seat licenses with automated workflow volume.

The reported numbers show both the promise and the emerging friction. For the quarter ended June 30, subscription revenue reached $3.88 billion, up 24.5%, while current remaining performance obligations hit $13.20 billion. But management's outlook points to deceleration, guiding September quarter subscription growth to 20.5% and obligation expansion to 19.5% against a $35 million currency drag. Leadership also conceded that the summer beat was flattered by federal agencies pulling software orders forward out of the autumn.

The bear case writes itself. You paid 42% more for an equity whose earnings revisions barely budged, leaving the valuation exposed if execution wobbles. Underlying cash quality reveals significant strain. While adjusted operating margin reached 29.5%, GAAP operating margin was just 4%, eroded by $655 million in stock-based compensation that consumed 16.5% of revenue. Operating cash flow fell to $587 million from $716 million a year earlier, and free cash flow relied on a $161 million acquisition add-back to show growth.

The pricing shift is only half complete. The remaining half of new contract value still tracks human headcounts—the exact line item corporate buyers want AI to cut. Upstarts like Serval, commanding a $1 billion valuation, are already targeting legacy ticket volumes directly.

For the equity to re-rate, the company must prove non-seat pricing can permanently decouple revenue from headcount. The average analyst price target sits only a few percent above the current tape, showing that Wall Street views the equity as fully priced. ServiceNow needs to push non-seat deals decisively beyond the halfway mark to convince investors that automation expands budgets rather than cannibalizing them.

The proving ground arrives on Oct. 28, when ServiceNow reports third-quarter earnings after the closing bell. Investors will see whether that pulled-forward federal revenue created an autumn air pocket, or whether current performance obligations can clear the guided 19.5% hurdle.

Software seats are no longer a growth engine.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in NOW. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
